title: A day of renunciation
hookLine: plain food, nothing to watch, and an old phrase for living lightly.
tomorrow: you've given, kept and let go. what's left to see clearly?

cards: Some people try a no-spend weekend, or a day without screens. So what is a whole day like with plain food and no entertainment?
The Buddha's teaching on kindness has an old phrase for the kind of person who could manage it, and it's not grim at all. In Pali: santussako ca subharo ca. Content, and easy to support.

teach.b: The line comes from the Metta Sutta, the discourse on loving-kindness.
Before it gets to wishing all beings well, it describes the person who does the wishing: able, upright, gentle, content and easy to support, with few duties, living lightly.
Contentment is listed right beside kindness, as if a person who needs less has more room for others.
The Dhammapada says it outright: contentment is the greatest wealth. That's what a day of renunciation tests. Plain food, so taste isn't running the day.
No entertainment, so attention comes home. The first hours can feel long.
That's not failure; it's the extra noise draining out.

teach.h: THE WHOLE WEEK, IN ONE DAY.
teach.b: This week's whole block sits inside it. You notice what others need, because you're not busy feeding yourself. You keep the precepts more easily, because there's less to grab for.
You let go, a little, and find out what it trades for.
A simple day isn't a lesser day. It's the same day with the clutter out of it.

how: Some lay Buddhists keep days of simplicity, sometimes on observance days, eating plainly and setting aside entertainment; the Metta Sutta, chanted in Theravada lands, names contentment among the qualities of a kind person.

games.q: what does “a day of renunciation” mean?
o: a fast with no food at all until sundown
a day spent giving away everything you own
a day of plain food and no entertainment, content

games.q: the week's six lines — tap the pairs.
p: the small pleasure for the great

s: a simple day is meant to be miserable on purpose
the Metta Sutta puts contentment right beside kindness. it's the same day with the clutter out.
the Metta Sutta describes the kind person as content and easy to support
santussako ca subharo ca: content, and easy to support, with few duties, living lightly.
renunciation only counts if it's permanent
a day counts, like the eight precepts kept for one day and night.

games.q: your cousin is doing a "simple day" and posts every plain meal online for likes. going by today's lesson, what's off?
o: nothing: plain food is plain food, posted or not.
the plainness has become a show; living lightly doesn't need an audience.
she should eat nothing at all to make it really count.
games.why: the Metta Sutta's person is content, with few duties, living lightly. a day of renunciation sets the audience down too.

practice: Look at what's around you right now and count three things that are already enough: the seat holding you, the water within reach, the light in the room. Name each one quietly. Then sit with the word enough for the rest of the bell.

wordCard.voice: A day of renunciation: plain food, no entertainment, and a mind content with little. Living lightly, for one day.

orig.note: Pali: contentment, being satisfied with little.

carryVoice: The line for today: simple day, the same day with the clutter out. Two weeks done; see you on the next page.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 1.8, Karaniya Metta Sutta (the one who would practice kindness: able, upright, gentle, content and easy to support, with few duties, living lightly)
